title: Pipelines and visible failure propagation
markdown:
## Why this matters

A pipeline connects the standard output of one command to the standard input of the next. The connection is a stream, not a contract about success: the last command can finish happily while an earlier stage failed to read its input at all. A counting command that prints `0` after a missing file is the classic case. This lesson makes every stage's status visible before you trust a number.

## The simple version

Picture a bucket brigade. Each person passes whatever arrives to the next; the last person reports "done" even when the first bucket was empty because the well was dry. Bash reports the status of the last command in a pipeline as `$?`. To learn about the well, you have to ask every person in the line, immediately, before they move on.

The analogy breaks in one way: unlike people, the stages run concurrently. A downstream command can start consuming before the upstream one has failed, so partial output is possible.

## Core mechanics

`$?` after a pipeline is the exit status of the last command unless `pipefail` is set. `PIPESTATUS` is an array holding every stage's status in order, but it describes only the most recent pipeline and is replaced by the next command you run, including an `echo` you add to inspect it. Capture it on the same line or copy it into your own variable first.

`set -o pipefail` changes `$?` to the status of the rightmost failing stage, which makes a hidden reader failure visible to `if`, `&&` and `||`. It does not stop the downstream stages from running; it only changes what the pipeline reports afterwards.

A non-zero status is not always an error. `grep` exits with 1 when nothing matched and with 2 for a real problem such as an unreadable file. Read the manual page of each stage for the meaning of its statuses before treating them as failures.

## Failure modes

Adding `2>/dev/null` to quiet a stage also hides the evidence that would have explained a wrong count. Prefer capturing stderr to a file you can inspect. Using `$?` two lines after the pipeline reports the status of whatever ran in between. Enabling `pipefail` globally in an interactive shell can make legitimate "no match" results look like failures in scripts that check `$?` casually.

## Runnable experiment

Run this in Bash in a scratch directory. It creates no files and needs no elevated permissions. Predict each line before running it.

```bash
cat missing.log | wc -l
printf 'status=%s\n' "$?"
# 0: wc succeeded, so the pipeline "succeeded"
cat missing.log | wc -l; printf 'stages=%s\n' "${PIPESTATUS[*]}"
# stages=1 0: cat failed, wc succeeded
set -o pipefail
cat missing.log | wc -l; printf 'status=%s\n' "$?"
# status=1: the reader failure is now visible
set +o pipefail
printf 'a\nb\n' | grep -c a; printf 'status=%s\n' "$?"
# 1 then status=0: one match
printf 'a\nb\n' | grep -c z; printf 'status=%s\n' "$?"
# 0 then status=1: no match is status 1, not an error
```

## Practical exercise

Write a three-stage pipeline that reads a log file, filters ERROR lines and counts them. Run it against a present file, a missing file and an unreadable file (create one with `chmod 000`). For each run record the printed count, `$?`, and `PIPESTATUS` captured on the same line. Then enable `pipefail` and repeat. Explain which runs produced a misleading count and which mechanism exposed each failure.

key_takeaways: After a pipeline, $? is the last stage's status unless pipefail is set.
PIPESTATUS describes only the most recent pipeline; capture it immediately.
A non-zero status means what that command's manual says, not always an error.

exercise.title: Make every pipeline stage's status visible
exercise.instructions: Write a three-stage pipeline that reads a log file, filters ERROR lines and counts them. Run it against a present file, a missing file and an unreadable file. For each run record the count, $? and PIPESTATUS captured on the same line, then repeat with pipefail enabled and explain which runs were misleading.
exercise.deliverable: A transcript of six runs (three files, pipefail off and on) with counts, statuses and a short explanation of each misleading result.
hints: Capture PIPESTATUS on the same line as the pipeline or it describes your next command.
grep exits 1 for no match; decide whether that is a failure for your report.
Keep stderr visible or redirect it to a file you inspect; do not discard it.

questions.prompt: After `cat missing.log | wc -l`, what does `$?` report by default?
choices: The highest status of any stage
The number of stages that failed
questions.explanation: Without pipefail, a pipeline's status is the exit status of its last command.
questions.learning_objective: Read a pipeline's default status correctly

choices: Downstream stages stop when an upstream stage fails
$? becomes the status of the rightmost failing stage
PIPESTATUS is cleared after each command
questions.correct_answer: $? becomes the status of the rightmost failing stage
questions.explanation: pipefail changes only what the pipeline reports; the stages still run.
questions.learning_objective: Explain what pipefail does and does not do

questions.prompt: Why can `echo "${PIPESTATUS[*]}"` on the next line show a wrong value?
choices: The array is replaced by the most recent command, including that echo
Arrays cannot hold more than one status
questions.correct_answer: The array is replaced by the most recent command, including that echo
questions.explanation: PIPESTATUS describes the last pipeline run; inspect it on the same line or copy it first.
questions.learning_objective: Capture PIPESTATUS at the right moment

questions.prompt: `printf 'a\n' | grep -c z` prints 0 and exits with status 1. What happened?
questions.correct_answer: No line matched, which grep reports as status 1. grep uses status 1 for no match and 2 for errors such as unreadable files.
questions.explanation: grep uses status 1 for no match and 2 for errors such as unreadable files.
questions.learning_objective: Interpret a stage's status from its documentation

questions.prompt: A report shows 0 errors after `cat app.log | grep ERROR | wc -l`, but the file was missing. Explain why the count looked valid and how you would expose the failure.
questions.correct_answer: cat failed with a non-zero status, but wc read empty input and succeeded, so $? was 0 and the count was 0. Capture PIPESTATUS on the same line or enable pipefail so the pipeline reports cat's failure; keep cat's stderr visible.
questions.explanation: The last stage's success masked the reader failure; PIPESTATUS or pipefail makes it visible.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose a hidden upstream failure in a pipeline
